course_description:
In this compulsory capstone course students consolidate and deploy writing skills first encountered in other courses in the major in order to complete a significant short work in a genre of their choice.

Building on the conceptual knowledge and practical skills that you have acquired in first- and second-year creative writing and/or professional writing units, in WRIT3000 Writing: Advanced Project you will plan, propose and write an advanced creative writing project, with an emphasis on furthering your project management and creative research skills.

Across the semester you will read and view a range of short works by leading Australian and international creatives working in the genres covered by the course — fiction, creative non-fiction, and screenplay excerpts and film. These weekly readings deliberately span diverse narrative perspectives, including the work of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers and filmmakers. We engage with them critically and respectfully as part of your development as a writer. There will also be lectures and guest talks by leading Australian industry professionals. You will meet in your tutorial groups for intensive, sustained workshopping sessions with your writing peers, led by an experienced creative writing tutor.

The genres available to you are fiction, creative non-fiction, and screenwriting. Before the first week of the course you will choose which genre to write in, and you will be placed into the appropriate workshop group.

Your creative work will either be a complete, self-contained piece of writing, or an excerpt from a longer work. A self-contained piece of writing could include:

An excerpt from a longer work could include:

WRIT3000 Writing: Advanced Project will introduce students to a writer's necessary practices in project management and manuscript development, creative research, intensive rewriting, revision, structural editing, line-editing, proofreading, and understanding the publishing and/or screenwriting industry.

PLEASE NOTE:

This is a hands-on, practical course, with less reading content and more time dedicated to student writing, discussion and workshopping. As such, your in-person attendance is critical to your success in this subject, as are your English language written and spoken skills.

Lectures in this course are not recorded for delayed viewing , as eight of the weekly lectures include an in-lecture writing exercise that must be completed in person under timed conditions. Please plan to attend all lectures and tutorials.

course_aims: Writing: Advanced Project supports you as you develop and completeﾠa substantial piece of writingﾠtoﾠa standard suitable for publication or production. You will study, apply and seek to masterﾠspecificﾠliterary techniques, in a genre of your choice. There is also a focus on project management, research, manuscript development and pitching your work to publishers and/or film production companies.

learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate mastery of key theories and practices in your chosen genre/format while engaging respectfully with diverse narrative perspectives, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives, across writing, publishing, and production contexts.
Develop advanced research and project management skills.
Provide contextualised, constructive feedback to industry standard.
Revise, edit and proofread to industry standard.
Identify key principles and emerging trends in the publishing and film production industries.

assessment_details.title: 2. In-Lecture Writing Exercises
assessment_details.other_conditions: Time limited, Secure. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Task description — Writing Exercise Assessment, based on lecture material. Completed in the lecture, in 20 minutes. From Week 2 to Week 11 there will be a written exercise held in the lecture (8 exercises in total). During the lecture you will be given 20 minutes to handwrite 150 to 200 words of creative writing responding to a specific concept raised in that week's lecture material. There are 8 opportunities across the semester, each worth 6%. Only your best 5 results count, together forming 30% of your final grade. Because only 5 of the 8 count, the assessment already builds in the flexibility to miss up to 3 sessions — for illness or any other reason — with no penalty and no documentation required. There are no opportunities to re-take an individual exercise, and no alternative assessment is available except in the specific circumstances set out below. As this is an internal course, you must make yourself available to complete each exercise at the scheduled date, time and venue. These are handwritten, closed-book tasks: no written material, electronic material or electronic devices may be used. All such items must remain in your bag or under your desk, and all electronic devices must be switched off or in airplane mode. If a device emits any noise, you may be subject to an allegation of misconduct and the item may be confiscated for the duration of the exercise. You may bring suitable writing implements (in a clear container), water in a clear bottle with the label removed, and disposable earplugs. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools is not permitted for this task. Read full task description Hide full task description
assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
Submit written paper to course staff in the lecture, immediately after each exam is finished.
Deferral or extension
You cannot defer or apply for an extension for this assessment.
Alternative assessment and accommodations
If you have a Student Access Plan (SAP) relevant to this task, please contact the course coordinator as early as possible. Reasonable accommodations can be made for matters documented in your SAP (for example, if you are unable to handwrite under timed conditions).
The 3-session buffer described above is intended to cover ordinary absences. A separate make-up session is available only to students who, for a genuine and documented reason, miss more than 3 of the exercises — for example, a sudden or serious illness, or another documented cause requiring a lengthy absence. Missing 3 or fewer sessions is already covered by the best-5-of-8 structure and does not qualify for a make-up.
To be considered for a make-up session or any other alternative arrangement, you must contact the course coordinator with your documentation as soon as possible after the circumstances arise. One make-up session will be offered in the Week 13 lecture slot; if you are eligible, please ensure you are available.
If you miss more than 3 of the writing exercises for documented and approved reasons, one make-up session will be offered in the Week 13 lecture slot, in which you will complete your outstanding exercises over a period of 80 minutes. Missing 3 or fewer sessions is already covered by the best-5-of-8 structure and does not require a make-up. Please ensure you are available in Week 13 lecture time if you are eligible.

assessment_details.title: 3. Workshopping Participation
assessment_details.due_date: Participation will be assessed wholistically across ten tutorials
assessment_details.task_description: All students are expected to participate actively in course activities. Participation will be assessed wholistically through regular in-class writing tasks which can be further developed at home then brought to class for further workshopping and development. Participation is marked out of 10 at the end of semester against Marking Criteria published on Blackboard, informed by the tutor's weekly record across the ten graded tutorials. Marks reflect involvement in the learning of the group: participation, preparation of each week's workshop task, and the quality of feedback given to peers. Attendance alone does not earn marks. The mark reflects demonstrated engagement with the workshop process. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Week 1 Lecture - The Capstone Semester: What This Course Asks & Offers You Course introduction; explanation of assignments (including the weekly in-lecture writing exercises); project planning; how to workshop; ensuring you're in the correct tutorial group for your chosen genre.
Week 1: No Tutorials No tutorials in week 1, tutorials start from week 2.

Week 2 Lecture - The Proposal as a Working Document The Project Proposal (800-word proposal + 200-word writing sample); research scaffolding and project planning. Writing Exercise 1 Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Week 2 Tutorial - From Concept to Page: Planning & Research in Practice Proposal workshop; turning a project idea into a realistic plan. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Week 3 - NO Lecture - Writing Week No lecture and tutorials this week due to Ekka Public Holiday. Please use this time to continue researching, and start your advanced writing project. Learning outcomes: L02, L05
Week 3 - NO Tutorials - Writing Week No lecture and tutorials this week due to Ekka Public Holiday. Please use this time to continue researching, and start your advanced writing project.

Week 4 Lecture - What Research Can’t Give You Guest writer Dr Martine Kropkowski (Everywhere We Look, Ultimo Press 2024; Left Behind, 2025) examines the limits of the archive and the place of lived and cultural knowledge in the creation of Fiction, CNF, and film. Her work bridges empirical inquiry and felt experience, with essays in Griffith Review, Overland and The Conversation. The set text for this lecture is her book, Everywhere We Look, available via the course Talis link. Writing Exercise 2 Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Week 4 Tutorial Exercises in research activities. Workshopping begins.

Week 5 Lecture - First Sentences, Last Sentences: The Contract a Writer Makes with a Reader Openings and endings as the writer’s promise; how a piece earns its first and last line. Writing Exercise 3 Learning outcomes: L01
Week 5 Tutorial Workshopping with a focus on openings and endings.

Week 6 Lecture - Structure as Meaning Structure read as an authorial decision rather than a template: the shape of a story as part of what it means. Guest writer Jack Dann (internationally award-winning author and UQ Adjunct Senior Research Fellow) takes the clearest case: alternate history, where changing a single event restructures an entire world, and the story's architecture becomes its argument. Drawing on his Fiction Writer's Guide to Alternate History (Bloomsbury Academic, 2023), with considerations across prose and screen. Fiction Writer’s Guide to Alternate History is the set text, available via the Talis link. Writing Exercise 4 Learning outcomes: L01, L05
Week 6 Tutorial Workshopping.

Week 7 Lecture - Voice, Authority, and Moral Position (or Not) Voice and the question of who may tell what: cultural authority, appropriation, and the ethics of representation. Writing Exercise 5 Learning outcomes: L01, L05
Week 7 Tutorial Workshopping

Week 8 Lecture - Authorship as Collaboration: AI as the (In)Visible Case AI and authorship as the live edge of an old question; emerging industry and legal context. Writing Exercise 6 Learning outcomes: L01, L04, L05
Week 8 Tutorial Discussion of the use of AI. Workshopping continues.

Week 9 Lecture - The Personal in Telling True Stories With guest writer Carly-Jay (CJ) Metcalfe , author of Breath (UQP 2024, winner of the 2024 Queensland Literary Awards People’s Choice Book of the Year) and UQ MPhil candidate. CJ will discuss memoir, the self on the page, and the ethics of writing real lives: her own and those of others. Breath is the set text, available via the Talis link. Writing Exercise 7 Learning outcomes: L01, L05
Week 9 Tutorial Discussion around the use of true stories; memoir or the lives of others. Workshopping.
Mid-Semester Break - No Classes

Week 10 - No Lecture - Writing Week Due to the King's Birthday public holiday, there are no lectures or tutorials this week. Please work on your drafts for final submission. Rewriting is key! Learning outcomes: L01, L04
Week 10 - No Tutorial - Writing Week Due to the King's Birthday public holiday, there are no lectures or tutorials this week. Please work on your drafts for final submission. Rewriting is key!

Week 11 Lecture - Revision as Confrontation: Reading the Story You Actually Wrote Revision, structural editing and proofreading to a professional standard; seeing the draft as it is, not as intended. Including "What we can learn from bad writing?" Writing Exercise 8 Learning outcomes: L01, L04, L05
Week 11 Tutorial Workshopping, with an emphasis on revision.
Week 12 Lecture - The Industrial Machine: Creating a Publishing and/or Filmmaking Journey Industry guest(s) (UQP + screen — TBC ); publishing and production pathways. Learning outcomes: L04, L05
Week 12 Tutorial - Copy Editing week Bring printed pages of the final project for peer proofreading; workshopping continues.

Week 13 Lecture - Writing Exercise Make Up Week This lecture slot will be used to host make up writing exercises for anyone who had documented approval to miss more than 3 exercises. Learning outcomes: L01, L04, L05
Week 13 Tutorial Bring printed pages of your final project for peer proofreading; workshopping continues in this final tutorial. Learning outcomes: L01, L04, L05

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Please allow 48 hours for a response - staff are often teaching or in meetings and cannot always reply on the same day. Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
